transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, to be honest, it’s... it’s kind of a long story. I mean, the main thing, what really brings me in today, is that ever since I stopped working—which, you know, everybody tells you is supposed to be this big relaxing time, right? You know, sit on the porch, take it easy, finally get some rest. But I just... I can’t seem to slow down. At all. 

I’m up and moving from the second my feet hit the floor in the morning, just going from one little job to the next, all day long. I’ll fix a squeaky hinge in the kitchen, and then before I even put the screwdriver away I’m out in the garage reorganizing boxes I haven’t looked at in a decade, and then I'm out back messing with the gutters. It’s like... well, it’s exactly like I still have a whole work crew waiting on me, you know? Like I've got guys standing around waiting for me to get the site ready or tell them what to do, so I just keep moving, moving, moving. 

My family tells me I need to just sit down and watch a baseball game or something, but I just keep finding these little projects. Before I know it, the whole day is gone and I haven't sat down in a chair once. It's just exhausting, but I just can't seem to hit the brakes.
Do you feel anxious or worried when you're not constantly busy with these projects?

Anxious? Worried? No, no, it’s not really like that. I mean, my wife, she actually asks me the exact same kind of thing. She’ll say to me, "What’s got you all worked up? What are you fretting about?" But I’m really not fretting at all. It’s not like I’m sitting there chewing my fingernails worrying about the electric bill, or thinking the roof is gonna cave in, or stressing over the grandkids or anything like that. My mind isn't spinning with worries. 

It’s more just... well, if I do try to force myself to sit down in the recliner—the big brown leather one the kids pitched in and got me for my retirement, really nice chair, actually, it's got the cup holders and the power recline and everything—if I sit in that chair to watch a game, I don’t feel scared or nervous. I just... I just feel like I need to get back up. My legs just sort of want to go. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly I'll think, "Hey, I should probably go check the air pressure on the truck tires." Not because I’m worried they’re flat! Just because it’s a thing to do, you know? A task. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm anxious at all. I don't lay awake sweating about the state of the world or anything. It’s just this motor inside me that doesn't seem to know I'm off the clock now. I just gotta be doing something.
Do you ever feel like you have to do these tasks or projects, like something is compelling you to keep going?

Compelling me? Like... like I *have* to do it, or else? No, no, it's not like that either. It's not like I've got a gun to my head or some voice telling me I have to go fix the fence right this second. It's just... well, like I was saying about the recliner. It's not a compulsion, I don't think. It's more just a restlessness, a need to be useful, maybe? 

Like yesterday, for example. I was out in the yard, and I saw that the old birdhouse my granddad built—the one that's been hanging on the oak tree for, gosh, must be thirty years now—it was looking a little worse for wear. The paint was chipping, the little perch was loose. Now, I didn't *have* to fix it. The birds didn't care. They were still using it just fine. But I just... I saw it, and I thought, "I can fix that." And the next thing I know, I've got the ladder out, I've got the sandpaper, I'm digging through the shed for that specific shade of blue paint I know I bought back in '15 when we did the trim on the guest room... 

It's not that I'm forced to do it. It's just that I see something that needs doing, and I just start doing it. And then one thing leads to another. I go to put the paint away, and I notice the shelf is wobbly, so I get the drill out for that, and then I see the drill battery is low, so I go to plug that in, and then I notice the outlet cover is cracked... You see what I mean? It's just a chain reaction of doing things. But it's not like I'm doing it against my will, or like I'm being driven by some outside force. It's just... me. Just me, always finding something to tinker with.
Do you often feel guilty when you're not working on these projects?

Guilty? Hmm... no, I wouldn't say I feel guilty. It's funny you ask that, though, because my daughter—she's a social worker over in the next county, always analyzing everybody, you know how they get when they do that kind of work—she said to me the other day, "Dad, do you feel like you have to earn your keep now that you're retired? Is that why you're always doing the yard work and fixing the neighbors' mowers?" 

But I told her, and I'll tell you, it's really not about guilt. I worked hard for forty-five years, put in my time, paid my taxes, raised three kids... I know I've earned the right to sit on my backside if I want to. I don't feel like I owe anybody anything, or like I'm doing something wrong if I'm not being productive. I don't sit there thinking, "Oh, shame on me, I should be out there painting the garage." 

It's really just what I was saying before. It's not guilt, it's just... I just don't like sitting still. If I do sit down, I don't feel bad about it, I just feel antsy. Like my legs are telling me, "Okay, we rested for five minutes, time to go check the oil in the lawnmower." It's a physical thing, almost. A restlessness. But no, no guilt. I know I'm officially a man of leisure now, even if my body hasn't quite gotten the memo yet!
Do you ever have thoughts that repeat over and over in your mind?

Thoughts repeating? Like a broken record? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like I get a song stuck in my head or keep thinking the same exact sentence over and over. My mind doesn't really get stuck in a loop like that. 

It's more like... well, it's like a television where somebody keeps flipping the channels. It's not the same show playing on repeat, it's a hundred different shows. Like I was saying about the birdhouse and the paint and the wobbly shelf. My thoughts don't repeat, they just jump. I'll be thinking about the birdhouse, and then suddenly I'm thinking about the weather, and then I'm wondering if I remembered to put the cap back on the weed whacker gas, and then I'm thinking about how the price of gas is just ridiculous these days, which makes me think of my old buddy Tom who used to own the filling station out on Route 9 before they built the bypass... 

You see? It's a whole string of different thoughts, moving real fast, one right after the other. But it's never just one thought playing over and over again, driving me crazy. It's more of a... a constant stream of new ideas of things I could be doing or fixing or checking on. So no, no repeating thoughts. Just a whole lot of different ones, moving at a pretty good clip.
Do you often act on these thoughts of fixing or checking on things without thinking them through first?

Act on them without thinking? Well... I guess it depends on what you mean by "thinking them through." I mean, I don't just go grabbing a chainsaw and hacking at the old oak tree without a plan, if that's what you're asking. I'm not reckless. I've still got all ten fingers, after all, which is more than my neighbor Dave can say after that incident with the table saw back in '98. 

But... do I sit down and draw up a blueprint before I tighten a loose screw on a cabinet door? No, course not. It's more like... I see it, I know how to fix it, so I just do it. Like the other day, I was walking through the kitchen to get a glass of water, and I noticed the hinge on the pantry door was squeaking. Just a little squeak, nothing major. Now, my wife, she'd probably put it on a list and say, "We'll get to that this weekend." But me? I heard the squeak, I turned right around, walked out to the garage, grabbed the WD-40, came back in, and sprayed it. Didn't even get my glass of water until after. 

So I guess I don't really stop to ponder it. The thought pops up—"Hey, that needs fixing"—and my feet are already moving before my brain has time to say, "Wait, shouldn't you finish what you were doing first?" It's just a reflex, really. Forty-five years of working with my hands, you see something broken, you fix it. You don't need a committee meeting to decide to oil a hinge or tighten a bolt. You just... do it. So, no, I wouldn't say I sit and analyze it. I just get to work.
Has your constant need to be busy and work on projects caused problems in your relationships or daily life?

Well, problems... I don't know if I'd call them *problems*, exactly, but... it definitely causes some friction. Mostly with my wife, Martha. Bless her heart, she's a saint, but I know I drive her up the wall sometimes. See, because I'm always jumping up to fix the squeaky hinge or check the lawnmower oil, I tend to forget the things I was actually supposed to be doing. 

Like, she's had to completely take over keeping the calendar. Used to be we'd both kind of manage it, but now? Forget it. If she doesn't write it down and stick it right on the refrigerator where I can't miss it, it just flies right out of my head. And even then, she's always having to check behind me. "Did you actually pay the water bill, or did you just get distracted fixing the leaky faucet?" That kind of thing. It's frustrating for her, and I get it, I really do. I feel bad that she feels like she has to manage me like one of the kids.

And it's not just at home, either. I try to stay active in the community, you know, since I retired. I volunteered to help out at the community center, setting up for events, and I joined the local community garden group—figured I could help them build some raised beds, maybe fix up their tools. But... well, I've had to apologize to both of those groups more than once. I'll promise to be at the center at 10:00 to set up chairs, but then on the way out the door, I'll notice the weather stripping on the front door is peeling, and the next thing I know, it's 11:30, I'm covered in old adhesive, and I've completely missed the setup time. I've definitely let people down, and that doesn't sit right with me. I've always prided myself on being dependable, you know? Forty-five years at the plant, I was never late. But now, it's like my brain just takes these detours, and I end up leaving people hanging. So, yeah, I guess it has caused some issues, even if I don't mean for it to.
Do you feel like your constant need to be busy and work on projects is affecting your overall happiness?

Happiness? Well... I don't know if I've ever really stopped to think about it in those terms. That’s a pretty big question. I mean, what is happiness, really, at my age? I’ve got my health, mostly, and I’ve got Martha, and we’ve got a roof over our heads that doesn't leak—well, mostly because I patched it up last spring after that big storm blew through. You remember that storm? The one that knocked down half the power lines over on Elm Street and took out the old willow tree at the park? 

Anyway, I wouldn't say being busy makes me unhappy. In fact, I think it’s what keeps me going. I like working with my hands. If I had to just sit in a recliner all day watching those daytime judge shows or the news, now *that* would make me miserable. My brother-in-law, Frank, he retired two years before I did from the auto shop, and all he does now is sit in his La-Z-Boy and complain about his knees. He’s absolutely miserable to be around. So having projects, having things to fix, it gives me a purpose, you know? 

But... I guess sometimes it does get a little tiring. Just a little. Like I was saying before about letting folks down at the community center, or Martha getting annoyed with me. That bothers me. And sometimes, I just want to be able to sit on the back porch and enjoy a cup of coffee without noticing that the wooden railing needs to be sanded and repainted. I'll sit down, coffee in hand, sun is shining, birds are singing, and I'll see this one little chip in the paint. And suddenly, I can't even taste the coffee anymore. I'm just staring at that chip, thinking about the moisture getting into the wood, and before I know it, I'm out in the shed looking for the sandpaper and the primer. And by the time I finally sit back down, my coffee is ice cold. 

Does that make me unhappy? I really couldn't tell you for sure. It's frustrating sometimes, sure, feeling like my engine is always running hot and I can't just put it in park. But I’ve never really sat down and asked myself if it’s ruining my happiness. I suppose I’ve just been too busy fixing the porch railing to think about it!
Have you always been this energetic and prone to taking on multiple tasks, or is this something that has developed more recently since your retirement?

Well, see, the thing is... I've always had a motor on me. You don't spend forty-five years doing handyman work and maintenance without having a bit of hustle, you know? When you're on the clock, bouncing from fixing a busted pipe in one building to patching up drywall in another, and then maybe climbing a ladder to clear out some gutters before the sun goes down... well, being energetic and juggling a bunch of tasks is just what they pay you for. It was just called being a hard worker. I had work orders, I had a boss, I had a schedule telling me exactly where to point all that energy. 

But as far as it actually being an issue? Like, getting in the way of my life, driving Martha crazy, or making me completely forget to show up for the community garden folks? That’s new. That really only became a real problem after I retired from the handyman work about a year and two months ago. 

I remember the exact time, too, because it was right around the end of October. I had just finished this awful job replacing exterior trim on a two-story colonial, wind howling, freezing my fingers off, and I just thought, "I am getting too old to be up on scaffolding in the winter." So I called it quits. Fourteen months ago. And you'd think, wouldn't you, that a fellow would just slow down? Sit back, read the paper, maybe do a little fishing. 

But without those work orders... man, it’s like I’m a wind-up toy that somebody cranked up all the way and then just took off the track. When I was working, I’d put in my eight or ten hours, come home, and I’d be too dog-tired to go hunting for squeaky hinges or peeling paint. The energy had a place to go. Now? Now it just spills out all over the house. I wake up at 6:00 AM, and if I don't have a list of official things to do, my brain just starts making up its own list, and before I know it, I've taken apart the toaster because the lever felt a little sticky. So, I guess I've always been a guy who likes to keep moving, but it didn't turn into this... this runaway train kind of situation until a year and two months ago when I finally handed in my keys.
Do you think your need to constantly be busy and work on projects is interfering with your ability to enjoy retirement or spend quality time with loved ones?

Well, enjoy retirement... I mean, everybody tells you retirement is supposed to be about kicking your feet up, right? Spending time with the family, sitting with your wife in the evenings. Martha, she absolutely loves her quiet evenings. She’ll get one of those thick mystery novels—she goes through them like water, I swear, gets them by the dozen from the library down on Main Street—and she just wants to sit in the living room with a cup of chamomile tea and read. And I try, Doc, I really do try to just sit there with her and enjoy that quality time. I figure, okay, I’ll pick up a book myself, or maybe do a little sketching. I used to like sketching out birdhouses or little woodworking plans, just quiet stuff, you know? 

But the truth is, I don’t do well with quiet hobbies for long anymore. It's like my body just completely rejects the quiet. I’ll be sitting there in my armchair, pencil in hand, or trying to read a chapter in some history book, and within ten minutes... well, I don't even realize I'm doing it at first, but I start humming. Just humming some old tune from the classic rock station. Or I start talking to myself out loud, muttering things like, "No, that angle's wrong, gotta rethink that joint," or "I wonder if we have any of those wood screws left in the coffee can." 

And Martha will just sigh and look over her reading glasses at me. Because even when I’m reading or sketching, I can't just sit and be still. If I'm not humming or talking to myself, I'm getting up to mess with something. I'll be trying to read, and I'll notice the lamp shade is just a fraction of an inch crooked, so I have to get up and adjust it. Then I notice the switch feels a little loose, so I'm off to the garage to get a screwdriver. And by the time I come back, the whole peaceful atmosphere is completely gone. So, yeah, I guess it really does interfere. I want to share those peaceful moments with her, I really do, but I just can't seem to get through a quiet evening without making a racket or bouncing out of my chair to tinker with the furniture.
Do you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh, boy... yeah. Yeah, I do. And it’s embarrassing, it really is. Martha actually convinced me to join this little group down at the community center—not the garden folks I mentioned earlier, but a different group. It’s a storytelling meeting they hold on Thursday mornings in the rec room. Just a bunch of us retirees sitting in a circle, you know, drinking lukewarm coffee and sharing stories from back in the day. The woman who runs it, Brenda, she picks a theme every week, like 'your first job' or 'the worst winter you remember,' and it’s supposed to be this nice, respectful thing where everyone gets their turn to speak. 

But... well, I just can't seem to hold my tongue. When I'm in those storytelling meetings, I'll answer or just jump right in before the other person even finishes. Like last week, George—he’s this retired postal worker, nice guy but he talks slower than molasses in January—he was telling us about his old Ford pickup, and he was trying to remember what kind of carburetor it had. And before he could even finish his sentence, I just blurted it out. I just jumped right in and took over his whole thought. And it's not just with facts or car parts, sometimes I'll just jump in with my own story before they even get to the punchline of theirs. 

The worst part is, the absolute second the words are out of my mouth, I realize I completely cut them off. I see George just kind of blink and lose his train of thought, and I just feel awful about it. I really do feel bad. I don't mean to be rude, I really don't! I'll sit there thinking, "Why couldn't you just wait two more seconds for the man to finish?" But it’s like the words are already out the door before my brain even has a chance to lock it. So then I end up apologizing, which just interrupts them all over again, and it makes a mess of the whole flow of the meeting. So, yes, I definitely do that, probably more than I should.
Do you have difficulty waiting for your turn in conversations or when doing activities with others?

Well, waiting... see, waiting is just about the hardest thing for me to do. It’s like torture, Doc. You’d think, being retired, I’ve got all the time in the world now, right? Nowhere to be, no boss breathing down my neck. But if I’m waiting in line at the hardware store—like down at Miller’s on 4th Street, where I’ve been getting my supplies for thirty years—and there’s even just one or two people ahead of me, I get so incredibly antsy. 

Just last Tuesday, I was in there to pick up some wood glue and a new pack of sandpaper, and this fella in front of me at the register was asking the cashier a million questions about which lawn fertilizer to use. And I’m just standing there, and I catch myself checking my watch every ten seconds. Then I’m looking at the clock on the wall, then back at my watch. I start shifting my weight from my left foot to my right foot, leaning on the counter, pacing a half-step out of line and back in. I just want to tap the guy on the shoulder and say, "Come on buddy, let's hurry things along!" 

And it's the exact same thing when I'm sitting for my turn at the clinic, like when I come in for these appointments or go to my regular doctor to get my blood pressure checked. They tell you to take a seat in the waiting room, and I just can't settle. I’m shifting around in those stiff chairs, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, picking up a magazine from three years ago and flipping through it without reading a single word. I just sit there wanting to push the whole process forward, maybe knock on the door and ask if they forgot about me. It’s this physical feeling, like a car engine running idle but it's starting to overheat, you know? So, yeah, waiting my turn, whether it's in a conversation or just standing in a line... I just don't have the patience for it anymore.
Have you experienced significant difficulties with organization and time management, such as keeping track of appointments or tasks, outside of your retirement and daily projects?

Well, organization and keeping track of things... no, I really wouldn't say I have much trouble with that at all. I mean, back when I was working, before I retired, I spent thirty-five years down at the auto parts manufacturing plant. I started right out of high school on the assembly line and eventually worked my way up to floor supervisor. And let me tell you, you absolutely could not be disorganized in that job. If you didn't manage your time down to the minute, the whole production line backed up and you had the plant manager breathing down your neck. I used to carry this little spiral-bound notebook in my front shirt pocket, just a little green one, and I wrote every single schedule and shift change in there. Never missed a meeting, never forgot a deadline. 

And even now, with doctor's appointments and all that, I stay right on top of it. Martha keeps this big wall calendar right next to the refrigerator in the kitchen. It is one of those free ones you get from the local bank at the end of the year. This year it has these beautiful pictures of old watermills on it, just gorgeous photography, really makes you want to take a road trip up to New England. Anyway, we write everything on there. If I have to get my blood pressure checked at two o'clock on a Tuesday, or if the truck needs its oil changed, it goes right on the calendar in blue ink. I check it every single morning while I am waiting for the coffee pot to finish brewing. I am usually the one reminding her about things, to be completely honest with you! Just last month she almost completely forgot her own sister's wedding anniversary, but I had it right there in my head and reminded her to buy a card. 

So, no, I really do not have a problem knowing where I need to be or keeping track of my appointments. My workbench out in the garage might look like a tornado hit it sometimes, with wrenches and sawdust all over the place, but my actual schedule? No, I have always been sharp as a tack when it comes to time. I just do not like waiting around once I actually get to the appointment, like I was saying before, but getting there on the right day and the right time is never an issue for me.
Have you ever had difficulty following through on instructions or failing to finish tasks due to distraction or losing interest?

Oh, well, yes. Yes, I do. And Martha will be the absolute first person to tell you all about it, let me tell you. It’s actually a bit of a running joke with us, except it’s not always so funny when it actually happens. 

We have this nice little house, got a good-sized yard, but keeping up with it is practically a full-time job in itself. Just this past weekend—Saturday, I think it was, because the weather was finally clearing up after all that rain we've been having—Martha gave me a very specific set of instructions for outside. She came out to the garage and said to me, very clearly, she said, "I need you to fix the side gate, sweep off the back porch, and make sure you put all the tools away when you're done." It sounded simple enough, right? Three things. One, two, three. 

So I go out there, and I start on the gate. It's this heavy old wooden gate, and the hinges get all rusted out and loose, so it sags and you have to physically lift the whole thing just to get the latch to close. I get my screwdriver and my WD-40, and I take the top hinge off. I've got the gate half done, propped up against my knee, and I happen to look down at the paving stones. And right there, growing up through the cracks in the walkway, are these awful dandelions and crabgrass. I just can't stand weeds, they make the whole yard look messy. 

So I think to myself, "I'll just pull this one big one right quick while I'm down here." I bend down, pull it, but the root snaps. So I have to dig at it a little. Then I see another one a few feet away, and another one over by the downspout. Next thing I know, I've wandered halfway across the yard, pulling weeds all along the side of the house, completely lost in what I'm doing. 

And the instructions she gave me? Completely gone from my head. I left the gate half done, just sitting there off its hinge. I never even made it over to the porch to get the broom to sweep it. And the tools? The screwdriver, the screws, the spray can—I just left the rest of it sitting right there in the dirt where I dropped them. Martha came out about an hour later to check on me, and she just sighed. Because there I was, elbow-deep in a patch of clover, and the gate was in worse shape than when I started. It’s not that I didn’t want to do what she asked, or that I was trying to ignore her instructions, I just... I get sidetracked by whatever catches my eye, lose all my interest in the first thing, and wander off into a completely different project.
Do you find it challenging to complete tasks because you lose interest or get distracted, even when you're doing something you enjoy?

Oh, absolutely. It doesn't even matter if it's something I really want to be doing, which is probably the most frustrating part of the whole thing. You know, since I retired from the plant, I tried to pick up a few quiet hobbies for indoors, just to keep my mind active, especially during the winter months when I can't be out in the garage as much. So I started doing a little watercolor painting, and I also like to sit and plan out these little mystery stories—just for myself, you understand, I'm no Hemingway or anything, but I really do enjoy figuring out the characters and the plots.

So, I'll get all set up at the kitchen table. I've got my brushes out, my little cup of water, maybe a fresh cup of coffee, and I'm really getting into it. I'm trying to paint, or I'm right in the middle of planning out a really good scene for my story. And then... well, say I hear a truck rumble by outside. We live on a corner lot, you see, so we get those big delivery vans taking the turn a little too fast, and they really rattle the front windows when they go past. Or, even if it's dead quiet in the house, I'll just suddenly think of something out in the garden. Like, I'll just be sitting there and out of nowhere I'll think, 'Oh, did I remember to check if the rabbits got under the chicken wire by the lettuce?' 

And the second that happens, my mind just jumps right over there. It completely leaves the kitchen table. I'll turn to look out the window to see what kind of truck it was, or I'll start running through a whole plan for reinforcing the garden fence in my head, and I completely lose where I was. I look back down at my notebook or my paper and I can't remember what color I was trying to mix, or what my characters were supposed to be doing next. The whole thought is just gone, evaporated into thin air. I can sit there for another twenty minutes trying to get the thread back, but usually my brain has just moved on, even though I was having a perfectly good time painting just a minute before.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or having trouble waiting for your turn in conversations?

Oh, Lord, yes. Yes, I do, and it is a terrible habit. You know how I was just telling you about those little mystery stories I like to plan out? Well, a few months ago, Martha told me I needed to socialize a bit more, get out of the house on weekdays so I wasn't just puttering around the kitchen, so I actually joined this little group down at the local library. We have these storytelling meetings every other Thursday afternoon in one of those back meeting rooms—the ones with the terrible fluorescent lights that always seem to be buzzing, you know the kind. 

There's about six or seven of us, mostly retired folks like me, and we just go around the table sharing what we're working on or asking for advice on our plots. It’s a real nice group of people, very supportive. But, well, this is exactly where I get myself into trouble. We’ll be sitting there, and someone will be explaining a scene, or maybe they're asking the group a question about how a character should react, and before I even realize what I'm doing, I’ll just answer or jump right in before the other person even finishes what they were saying. 

It's like the thought just pops into my head and shoots straight out of my mouth before I can put the brakes on. I don't mean to be rude, I really don't. I was raised better than that. But the second the words are out, I look at their face and realize I completely cut them off right in the middle of their sentence. I always feel just awful about it, I really do. I end up apologizing all over the place, saying, "I'm so sorry, go ahead, please finish," but the damage is already done, you know? It just slips out because I get so excited about the idea, or I think I know exactly what they're going to say, and I just can't seem to hold it in and wait my turn to speak. I do it to Martha sometimes, too, at the dinner table, and she just gives me this look over her glasses.
Do you often feel like you are doing things on impulse without fully thinking them through?

Impulse? Hmm. You mean like just up and doing something out of the blue without a second thought? No, I really do not think I do that. In fact, Martha would probably tell you I spend way too much time thinking about things before I actually get around to doing them. 

Like, just the other week, we needed a new toaster. The old one, the lever just would not stay down anymore. You would push it and it would just pop right back up, so you had to stand there and physically hold the plastic knob down if you wanted your bread browned at all, which is just a hazard if you ask me. Anyway, I did not just run out to the hardware store and grab the first one I saw on impulse. Oh no. I sat in my armchair in the living room for a good three days, looking up all the different models on my tablet, reading the customer reviews, comparing the slot sizes because I like those thick-cut bagels from the bakery downtown and you really need the extra wide slots for those or they get stuck and burn. I thought the whole purchase through completely from top to bottom. 

I mean, sure, like I said earlier, I might get distracted once I actually start a project in the yard, or I might speak out of turn at the library group, but as far as just making rash decisions or doing things on a whim without thinking? No, I do not really operate like that. I am actually pretty careful about planning my actions out, even if the plan kind of falls apart later on when I get sidetracked by weeds or what have you. But the initial action itself? No, I would not say I do things on impulse at all. I am a bit too set in my ways for that kind of excitement, I suppose.
Do you think your difficulty in focusing and constant need to be busy is related to your retirement or is it something you've experienced throughout your life?

Well, you know, Martha actually asked me that exact same thing a while back. She thought maybe because I wasn't at the plant anymore, punching the clock and having the foreman lay out exactly what I needed to be doing every hour of the shift, that my brain just didn't know what to do with all the free time. And I suppose that makes a certain kind of sense, right? You work for over forty years, you stop, and the engine just wants to keep running.

target_item.manifestation: Waiting in line at the hardware store or sitting for my turn at the clinic makes me antsy, and I catch myself checking the time, shifting around, and wanting to hurry things along.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have difficulty waiting my turn in conversations or activities, which directly aligns with the 'Waiting_Turn_Difficulty' symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, waiting... see, waiting is just about the hardest thing for me to do. It’s like torture, Doc. You’d think, being retired, I’ve got all the time in the world now, right? Nowhere to be, no boss breathing down my neck. But if I’m waiting in line at the hardware store—like down at Miller’s on 4th Street, where I’ve been getting my supplies for thirty years—and there’s even just one or two people ahead of me, I get so incredibly antsy. 

Just last Tuesday, I was in there to pick up some wood glue and a new pack of sandpaper, and this fella in front of me at the register was asking the cashier a million questions about which lawn fertilizer to use. And I’m just standing there, and I catch myself checking my watch every ten seconds. Then I’m looking at the clock on the wall, then back at my watch. I start shifting my weight from my left foot to my right foot, leaning on the counter, pacing a half-step out of line and back in. I just want to tap the guy on the shoulder and say, "Come on buddy, let's hurry things along!" 

And it's the exact same thing when I'm sitting for my turn at the clinic, like when I come in for these appointments or go to my regular doctor to get my blood pressure checked. They tell you to take a seat in the waiting room, and I just can't settle. I’m shifting around in those stiff chairs, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, picking up a magazine from three years ago and flipping through it without reading a single word. I just sit there wanting to push the whole process forward, maybe knock on the door and ask if they forgot about me. It’s this physical feeling, like a car engine running idle but it's starting to overheat, you know? So, yeah, waiting my turn, whether it's in a conversation or just standing in a line... I just don't have the patience for it anymore.

patient.answer:
Well, organization and keeping track of things... no, I really wouldn't say I have much trouble with that at all. I mean, back when I was working, before I retired, I spent thirty-five years down at the auto parts manufacturing plant. I started right out of high school on the assembly line and eventually worked my way up to floor supervisor. And let me tell you, you absolutely could not be disorganized in that job. If you didn't manage your time down to the minute, the whole production line backed up and you had the plant manager breathing down your neck. I used to carry this little spiral-bound notebook in my front shirt pocket, just a little green one, and I wrote every single schedule and shift change in there. Never missed a meeting, never forgot a deadline. 

And even now, with doctor's appointments and all that, I stay right on top of it. Martha keeps this big wall calendar right next to the refrigerator in the kitchen. It is one of those free ones you get from the local bank at the end of the year. This year it has these beautiful pictures of old watermills on it, just gorgeous photography, really makes you want to take a road trip up to New England. Anyway, we write everything on there. If I have to get my blood pressure checked at two o'clock on a Tuesday, or if the truck needs its oil changed, it goes right on the calendar in blue ink. I check it every single morning while I am waiting for the coffee pot to finish brewing. I am usually the one reminding her about things, to be completely honest with you! Just last month she almost completely forgot her own sister's wedding anniversary, but I had it right there in my head and reminded her to buy a card. 

So, no, I really do not have a problem knowing where I need to be or keeping track of my appointments. My workbench out in the garage might look like a tornado hit it sometimes, with wrenches and sawdust all over the place, but my actual schedule? No, I have always been sharp as a tack when it comes to time. I just do not like waiting around once I actually get to the appointment, like I was saying before, but getting there on the right day and the right time is never an issue for me.

doctor.question: Have you ever had difficulty following through on instructions or failing to finish tasks due to distraction or losing interest?

target_item.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: My wife can ask me to fix the gate, sweep the porch, and put the tools away, and I’ll get the gate half done, wander off to pull weeds, and leave the rest sitting there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty following through on instructions or failing to finish tasks, which directly matches the description of Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty.

patient.answer:
Oh, well, yes. Yes, I do. And Martha will be the absolute first person to tell you all about it, let me tell you. It’s actually a bit of a running joke with us, except it’s not always so funny when it actually happens. 

We have this nice little house, got a good-sized yard, but keeping up with it is practically a full-time job in itself. Just this past weekend—Saturday, I think it was, because the weather was finally clearing up after all that rain we've been having—Martha gave me a very specific set of instructions for outside. She came out to the garage and said to me, very clearly, she said, "I need you to fix the side gate, sweep off the back porch, and make sure you put all the tools away when you're done." It sounded simple enough, right? Three things. One, two, three. 

So I go out there, and I start on the gate. It's this heavy old wooden gate, and the hinges get all rusted out and loose, so it sags and you have to physically lift the whole thing just to get the latch to close. I get my screwdriver and my WD-40, and I take the top hinge off. I've got the gate half done, propped up against my knee, and I happen to look down at the paving stones. And right there, growing up through the cracks in the walkway, are these awful dandelions and crabgrass. I just can't stand weeds, they make the whole yard look messy. 

So I think to myself, "I'll just pull this one big one right quick while I'm down here." I bend down, pull it, but the root snaps. So I have to dig at it a little. Then I see another one a few feet away, and another one over by the downspout. Next thing I know, I've wandered halfway across the yard, pulling weeds all along the side of the house, completely lost in what I'm doing. 

And the instructions she gave me? Completely gone from my head. I left the gate half done, just sitting there off its hinge. I never even made it over to the porch to get the broom to sweep it. And the tools? The screwdriver, the screws, the spray can—I just left the rest of it sitting right there in the dirt where I dropped them. Martha came out about an hour later to check on me, and she just sighed. Because there I was, elbow-deep in a patch of clover, and the gate was in worse shape than when I started. It’s not that I didn’t want to do what she asked, or that I was trying to ignore her instructions, I just... I get sidetracked by whatever catches my eye, lose all my interest in the first thing, and wander off into a completely different project.

doctor.question: Do you find it challenging to complete tasks because you lose interest or get distracted, even when you're doing something you enjoy?

target_item.name: Distractibility

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about getting distracted during activities, even enjoyable ones. This maps perfectly to the Distractibility symptom, where I get distracted by outside noises or unrelated thoughts while trying to paint or plan a story.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It doesn't even matter if it's something I really want to be doing, which is probably the most frustrating part of the whole thing. You know, since I retired from the plant, I tried to pick up a few quiet hobbies for indoors, just to keep my mind active, especially during the winter months when I can't be out in the garage as much. So I started doing a little watercolor painting, and I also like to sit and plan out these little mystery stories—just for myself, you understand, I'm no Hemingway or anything, but I really do enjoy figuring out the characters and the plots.

So, I'll get all set up at the kitchen table. I've got my brushes out, my little cup of water, maybe a fresh cup of coffee, and I'm really getting into it. I'm trying to paint, or I'm right in the middle of planning out a really good scene for my story. And then... well, say I hear a truck rumble by outside. We live on a corner lot, you see, so we get those big delivery vans taking the turn a little too fast, and they really rattle the front windows when they go past. Or, even if it's dead quiet in the house, I'll just suddenly think of something out in the garden. Like, I'll just be sitting there and out of nowhere I'll think, 'Oh, did I remember to check if the rabbits got under the chicken wire by the lettuce?' 

And the second that happens, my mind just jumps right over there. It completely leaves the kitchen table. I'll turn to look out the window to see what kind of truck it was, or I'll start running through a whole plan for reinforcing the garden fence in my head, and I completely lose where I was. I look back down at my notebook or my paper and I can't remember what color I was trying to mix, or what my characters were supposed to be doing next. The whole thought is just gone, evaporated into thin air. I can sit there for another twenty minutes trying to get the thread back, but usually my brain has just moved on, even though I was having a perfectly good time painting just a minute before.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I interrupt others or have trouble waiting my turn in conversations, which matches the symptom of blurting out answers and cutting people off.

patient.answer:
Oh, Lord, yes. Yes, I do, and it is a terrible habit. You know how I was just telling you about those little mystery stories I like to plan out? Well, a few months ago, Martha told me I needed to socialize a bit more, get out of the house on weekdays so I wasn't just puttering around the kitchen, so I actually joined this little group down at the local library. We have these storytelling meetings every other Thursday afternoon in one of those back meeting rooms—the ones with the terrible fluorescent lights that always seem to be buzzing, you know the kind. 

There's about six or seven of us, mostly retired folks like me, and we just go around the table sharing what we're working on or asking for advice on our plots. It’s a real nice group of people, very supportive. But, well, this is exactly where I get myself into trouble. We’ll be sitting there, and someone will be explaining a scene, or maybe they're asking the group a question about how a character should react, and before I even realize what I'm doing, I’ll just answer or jump right in before the other person even finishes what they were saying. 

It's like the thought just pops into my head and shoots straight out of my mouth before I can put the brakes on. I don't mean to be rude, I really don't. I was raised better than that. But the second the words are out, I look at their face and realize I completely cut them off right in the middle of their sentence. I always feel just awful about it, I really do. I end up apologizing all over the place, saying, "I'm so sorry, go ahead, please finish," but the damage is already done, you know? It just slips out because I get so excited about the idea, or I think I know exactly what they're going to say, and I just can't seem to hold it in and wait my turn to speak. I do it to Martha sometimes, too, at the dinner table, and she just gives me this look over her glasses.

patient.answer:
Impulse? Hmm. You mean like just up and doing something out of the blue without a second thought? No, I really do not think I do that. In fact, Martha would probably tell you I spend way too much time thinking about things before I actually get around to doing them. 

Like, just the other week, we needed a new toaster. The old one, the lever just would not stay down anymore. You would push it and it would just pop right back up, so you had to stand there and physically hold the plastic knob down if you wanted your bread browned at all, which is just a hazard if you ask me. Anyway, I did not just run out to the hardware store and grab the first one I saw on impulse. Oh no. I sat in my armchair in the living room for a good three days, looking up all the different models on my tablet, reading the customer reviews, comparing the slot sizes because I like those thick-cut bagels from the bakery downtown and you really need the extra wide slots for those or they get stuck and burn. I thought the whole purchase through completely from top to bottom. 

I mean, sure, like I said earlier, I might get distracted once I actually start a project in the yard, or I might speak out of turn at the library group, but as far as just making rash decisions or doing things on a whim without thinking? No, I do not really operate like that. I am actually pretty careful about planning my actions out, even if the plan kind of falls apart later on when I get sidetracked by weeds or what have you. But the initial action itself? No, I would not say I do things on impulse at all. I am a bit too set in my ways for that kind of excitement, I suppose.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, Martha actually asked me that exact same thing a while back. She thought maybe because I wasn't at the plant anymore, punching the clock and having the foreman lay out exactly what I needed to be doing every hour of the shift, that my brain just didn't know what to do with all the free time. And I suppose that makes a certain kind of sense, right? You work for over forty years, you stop, and the engine just wants to keep running. 

But... no. No, if I am being completely honest with myself, and with you, this isn't a new thing at all. It is not just the retirement. It has been this way my entire life, clear back to when I was just a little guy. 

I mean, going all the way back to grade school, I remember my mother used to keep all my old report cards in this old shoebox up on the top shelf of the hall closet. And every single one of them, from Mrs. Gable in second grade all the way up, they all said practically the exact same thing. The teachers would write these little notes in the margins—in that nice cursive they used to teach back then—saying that I was a bright boy, but just completely scattered. 

I was always losing my things, for one. Pencils, especially. My mother must have bought me a hundred of those yellow number two pencils every single semester because I would set them down on my desk, look away for two seconds to see what the kid next to me was doing, and they would just vanish into thin air. And the calling out... well, just like I was telling you about the library group earlier, I was doing that at eight years old, too. The teacher would ask a question about spelling or arithmetic, and I would just blurt the answer right out from the middle row before she even had a chance to call on anybody who had their hand raised. 

And they were always, always having to stand over me, tapping on my desk, giving me reminders to finish my work before recess. Because if they didn't stand right there and remind me to focus on my paper, I would just be staring out the window at the swing sets, or fiddling with the hinge on my desk, and I would never get my assignments done before the bell rang. So, no, it is definitely not just since I retired. It has always been there, right from the start. I suppose it is just more noticeable to me now because I am actually supposed to be sitting back and relaxing for once, and I just can't seem to manage it.

patient.answer:
Well, it’s... you know, it’s a hard thing to admit, but yes. It really has. At the plant, like I was saying before, I had the foreman breathing down my neck, so I managed to keep my job and bring home a paycheck, even if I was always the guy leaving his wrench at the wrong station or forgetting his lunch pail in the truck. But in my personal life? My marriage? It’s been a real burden on Martha for decades, long before I ever retired. 

I mean, she has completely had to take over keeping the calendar for us. Every single doctor’s visit, every anniversary, when the property taxes are due, when the grandkids have a school play... she handles all of it. She keeps this big floral planner right by the telephone in the kitchen, and she is constantly having to check behind me to make sure I actually looked at it or did what I was supposed to do. If she didn't check up on me, I’d just drift off and forget half the things I promised to handle. It makes me feel like a child sometimes, having my wife double-check my chores, but... well, she has to, or things just fall apart. I'd forget to pay the water bill or I'd double-book us for a Sunday dinner.

And it’s not just at home, either. Socially, it’s been downright embarrassing at times. I’ve had to apologize to the folks down at the community center more than once. And the garden group, too! I’ll tell them, "Oh, sure, I’ll bring the extra bags of potting soil on Saturday," or "I’ll be there at eight sharp to help set up the folding tables for the plant sale," and then... I just get sidetracked by something else in the garage, or I completely forget I even volunteered, and I just don't show up. I've let people down more than once, and having to go back the next week, hat in hand, apologizing for being so unreliable... it really wears on you. People start to look at you like you just don't care about them, but I do care! I just... I can't seem to keep it all straight, and it’s been causing those kinds of headaches and hurt feelings for as long as I can remember.
